citations.quote:
Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root library's convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. The zero-dimensional space is excluded: its only endomorphism has trace $0$.

Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root convention that its inner product is linear in the first argument, and let $\rho$ be a density operator on $H$ ([[def-qc-density-operator]]). If $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d$ are its eigenvalues counted with multiplicity, define its **von Neumann entropy** by

$$S(\rho):=-\operatorname{tr}(\rho\ln\rho):=-\sum_{j:\lambda_j>0}\lambda_j\ln\lambda_j.$$

The trace is the finite-dimensional endomorphism trace ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]), and the spectral definition makes the expression independent of the eigenbasis. The term for a zero eigenvalue is defined to be $0\ln0:=0$. The default unit is nats, using the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]); the entropy in bits is $S_2(\rho):=S(\rho)/\ln2$.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $A,B:H\to H$ be non-negative operators. For such an operator $A$, set $\operatorname{supp}(A):=(\ker A)^\perp$, where $\ker A$ is the kernel of a linear map ([[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]); this extends the density-operator support convention in [[def-qc-density-operator]]. If $\operatorname{supp}(A)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(B)$, define

$$D(A\|B):=\operatorname{tr}(A\ln A)-\operatorname{tr}(A\ln B).$$

Here $\ln A$ is defined spectrally on the positive eigenspaces of $A$ with $0\ln0:=0$, and $\ln B$ in the cross term is restricted to $\operatorname{supp}(B)$; the support condition ensures that $A$ vanishes on $\ker B$, so the omitted kernel contributes zero. If $\operatorname{supp}(A)\nsubseteq\operatorname{supp}(B)$, set $D(A\|B):=+\infty$. In particular, $D(0\|B)=0$. For density operators this is the finite-dimensional **quantum relative entropy**. The logarithms are natural, so the value is in nats; the base-two value is $D_2(A\|B):=D(A\|B)/\ln2$.

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Let $H_A,H_B$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with fixed
ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For
$R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$ define
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

For nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$ and a density operator $\rho_{AB}$ on $H_A\otimes H_B$, both marginals $\rho_A:=\operatorname{Tr}_B\rho_{AB}$ and $\rho_B:=\operatorname{Tr}_A\rho_{AB}$ are density operators.

Let $H_G,H_Q$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces, and fix
the factor order $H_G\otimes H_Q$. For ordered orthonormal bases
$(g_s)$ and $(q_\alpha)$, define
$$\operatorname{Tr}_G:\mathcal B(H_G\otimes H_Q)\to\mathcal B(H_Q),\qquad (\operatorname{Tr}_G X)_{\alpha\beta}=\sum_sX_{(s,\alpha),(s,\beta)},$$
where $X_{(s,\alpha),(t,\beta)}=\langle X(g_t\otimes q_\beta),
g_s\otimes q_\alpha\rangle$ under the linear-first convention. Equivalently,
this is the partial trace over the second factor after swapping the two wires.
The partial-trace characterization and wire-permutation unitarity in
[[thm-qc-partial-trace-characterization-and-basis-independence]] and
[[thm-qc-wire-permutation-is-unitary]] show that the map is independent of
the chosen orthonormal bases. In particular, the same definition applies when
$H_Q=H_L\otimes H_R$, with that residual factor order left unchanged. For an
operator on $(H_G\otimes H_L)\otimes H_R$, use the canonical associator of
the ordered tensor-register construction to view it on
$H_G\otimes(H_L\otimes H_R)$ before taking this partial trace.

derivations.claim: By [F1], the input is a positive trace-one endomorphism on its finite tensor product. Apply [F5] to each bipartite grouping of a finite multipartite density operator; this makes every one-factor and two-factor marginal used in the Definition a density operator. Repeated partial traces use [F4] for the second factor and [F6] for the first factor, retaining the stated residual tensor-factor order.

Each such density operator has finitely many eigenvalues in $[0,1]$, so the finite entropy sum in [F2] is a real number, including when some eigenvalues vanish. The relative entropy clause is defined on exactly the two support cases in [F3]. Therefore $I(A:B)$ and $I(A:C\mid B)$ are finite real-valued functions on the stated density operators, and $D$ has the extended-real domain specified in the Definition.

boundaries.evidence: Trace one forces at least one positive density eigenvalue, so its entropy index set is nonempty. Relative entropy also permits X=0: its support is zero and the support-restricted trace is the empty sum zero under the stated convention;2.1 handles both support cases.
The Definition explicitly fixes 0 log 0=0 and assigns +infinity when relative-entropy support inclusion fails.
The finite spectral definitions include a one-dimensional density with its only eigenvalue equal to one, giving entropy zero.
The Definition uses the finite spectral trace and eigenvalues with multiplicity, so repeated eigenvalues do not select a preferred eigenbasis.

boundaries.reason: No variable parameter interval or limiting endpoint is part of these finite definitions.
Only finite-dimensional spaces and finite sums occur; no nonempty-family selection is asserted.

template_review.reason: Entropy is the support-restricted spectral sum in nats; partial traces in a fixed factor order define mutual and conditional information. These are definitions of quantities, not an equivalence to an independent predicate.

citations.quote:
All Hilbert spaces in this item are nonzero and finite-dimensional over $\mathbb C$. A density operator $\rho$ on $H$ is a Hermitian positive semidefinite endomorphism with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$. Its dimensionless von Neumann entropy, in nats, is

$$S(\rho):=-\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho)=-\sum_{j:\lambda_j>0}\lambda_j\log\lambda_j,$$

where $\lambda_j$ are the eigenvalues of $\rho$, the logarithm is natural, and $0\log0:=0$. For any positive semidefinite endomorphisms $X,Y$ on one finite-dimensional $H$, let $\operatorname{supp}X:=(\ker X)^\perp$. Define

$$D(X\|Y):=\operatorname{Tr}(X\log X)-\operatorname{Tr}(X\log Y)$$

when $\operatorname{supp}X\subseteq\operatorname{supp}Y$, taking each logarithm spectrally on its positive support and setting zero-eigenvalue contributions to zero; set $D(X\|Y):=+\infty$ otherwise. For density operators this is the finite-dimensional quantum relative entropy in nats.

For a density operator $\rho_{AB}$ on the ordered product $H_A\otimes H_B$, define $\rho_A:=\operatorname{Tr}_B\rho_{AB}$ and $\rho_B:=\operatorname{Tr}_A\rho_{AB}$, where in orthonormal product bases $\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B R\bigr)_{ii'}=\sum_jR_{(i,j),(i',j)}$ and the first factor is retained. Define

$$I(A:B)_\rho:=S(\rho_A)+S(\rho_B)-S(\rho_{AB}).$$

For a density operator $\rho_{ABC}$ on $H_A\otimes H_B\otimes H_C$, define

$$\rho_{AB}:=\operatorname{Tr}_C\rho_{ABC},\qquad
\rho_{BC}:=\operatorname{Tr}_A\rho_{ABC},\qquad
\rho_B:=\operatorname{Tr}_A(\operatorname{Tr}_C\rho_{ABC}),$$

where each partial trace contracts the indicated tensor factor and retains the other factors in their displayed order.

$$I(A:C\mid B)_\rho:=S(\rho_{AB})+S(\rho_{BC})-S(\rho_B)-S(\rho_{ABC}),$$

using the partial traces in the displayed factor order. For any fixed positive conversion factor $k_B$ with units J/K, the corresponding physical entropy is $S_{\mathrm{phys}}(\rho):=k_BS(\rho)$; no numerical value of $k_B$ is specified here.

Let $d,e\geq1$ be integers, let $H_{\mathrm{in}}=\mathbb C^d$ and $H_{\mathrm{out}}=\mathbb C^e$ with their standard inner products, and write $M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $M_e(\mathbb C)$ for the complex linear maps on these spaces. A matrix $X$ is **positive semidefinite**, written $X\geq0$, when it is Hermitian and $\langle Xv,v\rangle\geq0$ for every vector $v$. The finite spectral convention in [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]] gives positive matrices their orthonormal eigenbases and positive square roots.

A **positive map** is a complex-linear map $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ such that $\Phi(X)\geq0$ whenever $X\geq0$. For each integer $r\geq1$, identify $M_r(\mathbb C)\otimes M_d(\mathbb C)$ with matrices on $\mathbb C^r\otimes\mathbb C^d$ in the ordered product basis. The map $\Phi$ is **completely positive** when $\operatorname{id}_r\otimes\Phi$ is positive for every such $r$, where $\operatorname{id}_r$ is the identity map on $M_r(\mathbb C)$.

The map $\Phi$ is **trace-preserving** when $\operatorname{Tr}(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{Tr}(X)$ for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$. A **finite quantum channel** is a complex-linear map that is both completely positive and trace-preserving, abbreviated CPTP. Unitality, $\Phi(I_d)=I_e$, is a separate condition and is not part of this definition.

This is a mathematical definition. A physical preparation, measurement, or open-system model must separately identify when one of these maps represents a physical transformation.

Let $H_A,H_B,H_C$ be nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces and let $\rho_{ABC}$ be a density operator on their ordered tensor product. Write $\rho_{AB},\rho_{BC},\rho_B$ for its marginals using the partial traces in [[def-qc-partial-trace]]. Then
$$S(\rho_{AB})+S(\rho_{BC})\ge S(\rho_B)+S(\rho_{ABC}),$$
where $S(\rho)=-\operatorname{tr}(\rho\ln\rho)$ with $0\ln0:=0$ as in [[def-it-von-neumann-entropy]].

Let $H_A,H_B$ be nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces, let $d=\dim H_B\ge1$, and let $A,B$ be non-negative operators on $H_A\otimes H_B$. Then

$$D(\operatorname{Tr}_B A\|\operatorname{Tr}_B B)\le D(A\|B).$$

Let $d,e\geq1$ and let $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ be complex-linear. Choose the standard input basis $(|i\rangle)_{i=1}^d$, let $E_{ij}=|i\rangle\langle j|$, and use the ordered tensor convention input-reference $\otimes$ output. Define the (unnormalized) Choi matrix

$$J(\Phi):=\sum_{i,j=1}^{d}E_{ij}\otimes\Phi(E_{ij})\in M_d(\mathbb C)\otimes M_e(\mathbb C).$$ Then $\Phi$ is completely positive if and only if $J(\Phi)\geq0$, and this holds if and only if there are $q\leq de$ matrices $K_1,\ldots,K_q:\mathbb C^d\to\mathbb C^e$ such that $$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_aXK_a^*\qquad(X\in M_d(\mathbb C)).$$

The empty sum is allowed when $\Phi=0$. For any such Kraus representation, $\Phi$ is trace-preserving if and only if $\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_a^*K_a=I_d$.

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Let $H_A,H_B$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with fixed
ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For
$R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$ define
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $A,B:H\to H$ be non-negative operators. For such an operator $A$, set $\operatorname{supp}(A):=(\ker A)^\perp$, where $\ker A$ is the kernel of a linear map ([[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]); this extends the density-operator support convention in [[def-qc-density-operator]]. If $\operatorname{supp}(A)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(B)$, define

$$D(A\|B):=\operatorname{tr}(A\ln A)-\operatorname{tr}(A\ln B).$$

Here $\ln A$ is defined spectrally on the positive eigenspaces of $A$ with $0\ln0:=0$, and $\ln B$ in the cross term is restricted to $\operatorname{supp}(B)$; the support condition ensures that $A$ vanishes on $\ker B$, so the omitted kernel contributes zero. If $\operatorname{supp}(A)\nsubseteq\operatorname{supp}(B)$, set $D(A\|B):=+\infty$. In particular, $D(0\|B)=0$. For density operators this is the finite-dimensional **quantum relative entropy**. The logarithms are natural, so the value is in nats; the base-two value is $D_2(A\|B):=D(A\|B)/\ln2$.

Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

derivations.claim: By [A1], the left side of the first assertion is the displayed four-entropy difference. Apply [F1] to the given state with the same factor order; the resulting inequality is exactly $I(A:C\mid B)_\rho\ge0$.

By [F3], choose a finite Kraus list $K_1,\ldots,K_q$ with $\sum_aK_a^*K_a=I_d$; because $d\ge1$, this identity rules out $q=0$. Let $\mathcal E=\mathbb C^q$ with orthonormal basis $(f_a)$ and define $V:\mathbb C^d\to\mathbb C^e\otimes\mathcal E$ by $Vx=\sum_aK_ax\otimes f_a$. Orthogonality of the $f_a$ gives $\langle Vx,Vy\rangle=\sum_a\langle K_ax,K_ay\rangle=\langle x,(\sum_aK_a^*K_a)y\rangle=\langle x,y\rangle$, so $V^*V=I_d$. The coordinate formula [F4] then gives $\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathcal E}(VXV^*)=\sum_aK_aXK_a^*=\Phi(X)$ for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$.

The isometry $V$ maps each positive-eigenvalue eigenspace of $X\ge0$ onto the corresponding eigenspace of $VXV^*$, with the same eigenvalue; the orthogonal complement of $\operatorname{ran}V$ is in the kernel. Hence $\operatorname{supp}(VXV^*)=V(\operatorname{supp}X)$, and likewise for $Y$. Because $V$ is injective, support inclusion holds for $X,Y$ exactly when it holds for $VXV^*,VYV^*$. If it fails, both relative entropies are $+\infty$ by [F5]. If it holds, the support-restricted spectral logarithms satisfy $\log(VXV^*)=V(\log X)V^*$ and $\log(VYV^*)=V(\log Y)V^*$ on the corresponding supports. The trace identity in [F6] therefore yields $D(VXV^*\|VYV^*)=D(X\|Y)$.

Apply [F2] to $R=VXV^*$ and $S=VYV^*$, which are positive semidefinite because $V$ is linear and $X,Y\ge0$. By step 1.2 their partial traces are $\Phi(X),\Phi(Y)$, and by step 2.1 their relative entropy equals $D(X\|Y)$. Thus $D(\Phi(X)\|\Phi(Y))\le D(X\|Y)$, including when the right side is $+\infty$.

boundaries.reason: The theorem requires nonzero finite tensor factors and integers d,e>=1; zero-dimensional spaces are excluded.

Step 2.1 uses eigenspaces and supports, not a choice of basis inside degenerate eigenspaces.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.2 constructs a finite environment from the finite Kraus list; no arbitrary-index choice is used.

Neither inequality is stated as an iff.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For a trace-class density $\rho$ on a Hilbert space $H$, define its support subspace in either finite or infinite dimension by
$$\operatorname{supp}\rho:=(\ker\rho)^\perp,\qquad \ker\rho:=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}.$$
It is closed; write $P_\rho$ for its orthogonal projection, whose existence and uniqueness follow from [[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]].

Fix the positive Boltzmann scale $k_B>0$ (in SI units J/K, as in the approved QSM quantities design and [[lem-qsm-trace-state-calculus]]). For a trace-class density $\rho$ with positive eigenvalues $p_i$, define $S(\rho)=-k_B\sum_i p_i\log p_i\in[0,\infty]$, with $0\log0=0$. The logarithm is natural and acts on dimensionless density eigenvalues.

For finite-dimensional densities $\rho,\sigma$, define $\operatorname{supp}\rho=(\ker\rho)^\perp$. If $\operatorname{supp}\rho\not\subseteq\operatorname{supp}\sigma$, set $D(\rho\|\sigma)=+\infty$. Otherwise define
$
D(\rho\|\sigma)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho)-\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\sigma),
$
where each logarithm is restricted to the positive support of its operator and zero eigenvalues contribute zero to $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho)$.

For trace-class normal densities on a separable Hilbert space, write $\rho=\sum_i p_i|u_i\rangle\langle u_i|$ and $\sigma=\sum_j s_j|v_j\rangle\langle v_j|$ on their positive supports. Define the nonnegative cross-log moment
$
C(\rho,\sigma):=\sum_{i,j}p_i(-\log s_j)|\langle u_i,v_j\rangle|^2\in[0,\infty].
$
This is the spectral first moment of $-\log\sigma$ in the scalar state law of $\rho$; equivalently it is the nonnegative sum over the spectral projections, so it is independent of bases within eigenspaces. When support inclusion holds and $C(\rho,\sigma)$ and $S(\rho)$ are both finite, define $D(\rho\|\sigma)=C(\rho,\sigma)-S(\rho)/k_B$. If $C=+\infty$ and $S(\rho)<\infty$, set $D=+\infty$. No value is assigned by this definition to $+\infty-(+\infty)$; [[thm-qsm-trace-cross-log-inequality]] proves that finite $C$ forces finite $S(\rho)$.

The spectral-moment identification in the preceding cross-log clause is restricted to $\operatorname{supp}\rho\subseteq\operatorname{supp}\sigma$, so that the state is supported on the space where $-\log\sigma$ acts. Outside that domain, $C$ denotes only the displayed nonnegative double sum.

Let $H=H^*$ act on a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space of dimension $d\geq1$, $\beta>0$, $k_B>0$, $T=(k_B\beta)^{-1}$, and $Z=\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H})$. Put $\sigma=e^{-\beta H}/Z$, $F_\beta=-\beta^{-1}\log Z$, and $S(\rho)=-k_B\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho)$, with $0\log0=0$. Then every density matrix $\rho$, including rank-deficient matrices, satisfies
$
\operatorname{Tr}(\rho H)-TS(\rho)\geq F_\beta,
$
with equality if and only if $\rho=\sigma$. Moreover $S(\sigma)=k_B(\log Z+\beta\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma H))$, so $F_\beta=\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma H)-TS(\sigma)$. This is finite-dimensional mathematical optimization; actual preparation is a separate postulate.

For nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$ and a density operator $\rho_{AB}$ on $H_A\otimes H_B$, both marginals $\rho_A:=\operatorname{Tr}_B\rho_{AB}$ and $\rho_B:=\operatorname{Tr}_A\rho_{AB}$ are density operators.

Let $V,W$ be nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner product spaces with orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_m)$ of $V$ and $(f_1,\dots,f_n)$ of $W$, let $V\otimes W$ be their tensor product with the inner product of [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], and let $\operatorname{tr}$ denote the basis-independent trace of an endomorphism ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]).

(a) For every endomorphism $R$ of $V\otimes W$ there is a unique endomorphism $\operatorname{Tr}_W R$ of $V$ with

$$\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\operatorname{Tr}_WR)A\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(R(A\otimes I_W)\bigr)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\operatorname{End}(V),$$

namely $\operatorname{Tr}_WR=\sum_{j=1}^n\varphi_j\circ R\circ\iota_j$, where $\iota_j(v)=v\otimes f_j$ and $\varphi_j(x\otimes w)=\langle w,f_j\rangle x$; it does not depend on the orthonormal basis $(f_j)$ of $W$, and the analogous definition gives $\operatorname{Tr}_V R$ with $\operatorname{tr}((\operatorname{Tr}_VR)B)=\operatorname{tr}(R(I_V\otimes B))$.

(b) $\operatorname{Tr}_W$ is linear, positive (it maps positive endomorphisms to positive endomorphisms) and trace preserving on density matrices: if $R\ge0$ and $\operatorname{tr}R=1$ then $\operatorname{Tr}_WR\ge0$ and $\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Tr}_WR=1$; and $\operatorname{Tr}_W T_{\Psi,\Psi}=CC^*$ for every $\Psi\in V\otimes W$, where $C:W\to V$ is the coefficient map determined by $\Psi=\sum_jCf_j\otimes f_j$.

(c) *Schmidt decomposition.* Every $\Psi\in V\otimes W$ admits an expansion

$$\Psi=\sum_{r=1}^{k}s_r\,v_r\otimes u_r,$$

with $k\le\min(m,n)$, orthonormal families $(v_r)\subseteq V$, $(u_r)\subseteq W$ and $s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_k>0$ uniquely determined by $\Psi$ as the positive singular values of the coefficient map; moreover $\|\Psi\|^2=\sum_rs_r^2$. For $\|\Psi\|=1$ the reduced density $\rho=\operatorname{Tr}_W T_{\Psi,\Psi}$ satisfies $\operatorname{tr}\rho^2=\sum_rs_r^4$, and $\operatorname{tr}\rho^2=1$ holds exactly when $k=1$, i.e. exactly when $\Psi$ is a product vector; mixed-state separability is not decided by this criterion.

(d) *Finite nonselective no-signalling.* If $(M_a)_{a=1}^p$ are endomorphisms of $W$ with $\sum_aM_a^*M_a=I_W$ then for every endomorphism $R$ of $V\otimes W$

$$\operatorname{Tr}_W\Bigl(\sum_a(I_V\otimes M_a)R(I_V\otimes M_a^*)\Bigr)=\operatorname{Tr}_WR .$$

This is an identity for the specified finite local instrument; selective conditioning (dividing one summand by its nonzero trace) is not covered.

All Hilbert spaces in this item are nonzero and finite-dimensional over $\mathbb C$. A density operator $\rho$ on $H$ is a Hermitian positive semidefinite endomorphism with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$. Its dimensionless von Neumann entropy, in nats, is

$$S(\rho):=-\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho)=-\sum_{j:\lambda_j>0}\lambda_j\log\lambda_j,$$

where $\lambda_j$ are the eigenvalues of $\rho$, the logarithm is natural, and $0\log0:=0$. For any positive semidefinite endomorphisms $X,Y$ on one finite-dimensional $H$, let $\operatorname{supp}X:=(\ker X)^\perp$. Define

$$D(X\|Y):=\operatorname{Tr}(X\log X)-\operatorname{Tr}(X\log Y)$$

when $\operatorname{supp}X\subseteq\operatorname{supp}Y$, taking each logarithm spectrally on its positive support and setting zero-eigenvalue contributions to zero; set $D(X\|Y):=+\infty$ otherwise. For density operators this is the finite-dimensional quantum relative entropy in nats.

For a density operator $\rho_{AB}$ on the ordered product $H_A\otimes H_B$, define $\rho_A:=\operatorname{Tr}_B\rho_{AB}$ and $\rho_B:=\operatorname{Tr}_A\rho_{AB}$, where in orthonormal product bases $\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B R\bigr)_{ii'}=\sum_jR_{(i,j),(i',j)}$ and the first factor is retained. Define

$$I(A:B)_\rho:=S(\rho_A)+S(\rho_B)-S(\rho_{AB}).$$

For a density operator $\rho_{ABC}$ on $H_A\otimes H_B\otimes H_C$, define

$$\rho_{AB}:=\operatorname{Tr}_C\rho_{ABC},\qquad
\rho_{BC}:=\operatorname{Tr}_A\rho_{ABC},\qquad
\rho_B:=\operatorname{Tr}_A(\operatorname{Tr}_C\rho_{ABC}),$$

where each partial trace contracts the indicated tensor factor and retains the other factors in their displayed order.

$$I(A:C\mid B)_\rho:=S(\rho_{AB})+S(\rho_{BC})-S(\rho_B)-S(\rho_{ABC}),$$

using the partial traces in the displayed factor order. For any fixed positive conversion factor $k_B$ with units J/K, the corresponding physical entropy is $S_{\mathrm{phys}}(\rho):=k_BS(\rho)$; no numerical value of $k_B$ is specified here.

Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

For $m\geq1$ density matrices $\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_m$ on one finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space and weights $t_a\geq0$ with $\sum_at_a=1$, define their mixture $\rho:=\sum_at_a\rho_a$. The exact content of entropy concavity under finite mixing is
$$S(\rho)\geq\sum_{a=1}^m t_aS(\rho_a).$$
For density matrices $\rho,\sigma$ on finite-dimensional complex Hilbert spaces, the exact content of product additivity is $S(\rho\otimes\sigma)=S(\rho)+S(\sigma)$.

For the positive entropy scale $k_B>0$ fixed in [[def-qsm-relative-entropy-domain]] (in SI units J/K), entropy is concave under finite mixing and additive on product states for finite-dimensional density matrices. If $R$ is a density matrix on $H_A\otimes H_B$, with marginals $\rho_A=\operatorname{Tr}_B R$, $\rho_B=\operatorname{Tr}_A R$, then
$
S(R)\leq S(\rho_A)+S(\rho_B),
$
with equality exactly when $R=\rho_A\otimes\rho_B$. These finite statements include rank-deficient densities and assert neither strong subadditivity nor general infinite-dimensional data processing.

derivations.claim: By [F5], $H$ has finitely many real eigenvalues, so $e^{-\beta H}$ is positive definite and $Z_\beta>0$. Thus $\rho_\beta$ is a finite Gibbs density to which [F1] applies. Its marginals $\rho_A:=\operatorname{Tr}_B\rho_\beta$ and $\rho_B:=\operatorname{Tr}_A\rho_\beta$ are density operators by [F2].

Set $\tau:=\rho_A\otimes\rho_B$. Tensor products of orthonormal eigenbases show that $\tau$ is positive semidefinite with eigenvalues $p_iq_j$, whose sum is $(\sum_i p_i)(\sum_jq_j)=1$; hence $\tau$ is a density operator. By [F6], $S_{\mathrm{phys}}(\tau)=S_{\mathrm{phys}}(\rho_A)+S_{\mathrm{phys}}(\rho_B)$. Since $k_B>0$ and $S_{\mathrm{phys}}=k_BS$, division by $k_B$ gives $S(\tau)=S(\rho_A)+S(\rho_B)$. Therefore [F4] gives $S(\tau)-S(\rho_\beta)=I(A:B)_{\rho_\beta}$.

Define $F_\beta(\omega):=\operatorname{Tr}(H\omega)-\beta^{-1}S(\omega)$ for finite density matrices. Since $T S_{\mathrm{phys}}=T k_BS=\beta^{-1}S$, [F1] applies to this functional and yields $F_\beta(\rho_\beta)\le F_\beta(\tau)$. Rearranging and using step 2.1 gives $\beta^{-1}I(A:B)_{\rho_\beta}\le\operatorname{Tr}(H(\tau-\rho_\beta))$.

The coordinate formula in [F3] gives $\operatorname{Tr}_B(\rho_A\otimes\rho_B)=\rho_A$ and $\operatorname{Tr}_A(\rho_A\otimes\rho_B)=\rho_B$, since each factor has trace one. The defining trace-pairing identities in [F3], with cyclicity from [F5], then show that the expectations of $H_A\otimes I_B$ in $\tau$ and $\rho_\beta$ agree, and likewise for $I_A\otimes H_B$. Thus both local terms cancel in the trace on the right of step 3.1, leaving $\operatorname{Tr}(H(\tau-\rho_\beta))=\operatorname{Tr}(H_{\partial}(\tau-\rho_\beta))$.

Diagonalize $H_{\partial}=\sum_j\lambda_jP_j$ by [F5]. For any density matrix $\omega$, the numbers $w_j:=\operatorname{Tr}(P_j\omega)$ are nonnegative (each is a sum of nonnegative diagonal expectations of $\omega$ on an orthonormal basis of $\operatorname{ran}P_j$) and sum to one. Thus $|\operatorname{Tr}(H_{\partial}\omega)|=|\sum_j\lambda_jw_j|\le\sum_j|\lambda_j|w_j\le\max_j|\lambda_j|=\|H_{\partial}\|_{\mathrm{op}}$. Applying this absolute bound to $\tau$ and $\rho_\beta$ gives $\operatorname{Tr}(H_{\partial}(\tau-\rho_\beta))\le2\|H_{\partial}\|_{\mathrm{op}}$. Combine this with steps 3.1 and 4.1 and multiply by $\beta>0$ to obtain the claimed inequality. Substituting the additional family bound $\|H_{\partial}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le C|\partial A|$ yields its stated conditional area scaling.

derivations.claim: The vector $|\Phi\rangle$ has norm one because $|00\rangle$ and $|11\rangle$ are orthonormal, so $\rho_\Phi$ is a rank-one projection with trace one. The two orthogonal basis projections defining $\rho_{\mathrm{diag}}$ are positive and each has trace one, so their half-weighted sum is also positive with trace one. Expanding $\rho_\Phi$ gives the four terms $\tfrac12|00\rangle\langle00|$, $\tfrac12|00\rangle\langle11|$, $\tfrac12|11\rangle\langle00|$, and $\tfrac12|11\rangle\langle11|$. In the partial trace over the second factor, the two off-diagonal terms vanish because the traced basis indices differ, by [F2]; in the trace over the first factor, the same is true by [F4]. In both cases the diagonal terms each contribute one half of the corresponding basis projection, so both marginals are $I_2/2$. Applying the same two formulas to $\rho_{\mathrm{diag}}$ gives these marginals directly; they are density operators by [F3].

The eigenvalues of $\rho_\Phi$ are $1,0,0,0$, those of $\rho_{\mathrm{diag}}$ are $1/2,1/2,0,0$, and those of each marginal are $1/2,1/2$. Substitution into [F1] yields $S(\rho_\Phi)=0$, $S(\rho_{\mathrm{diag}})=\log2$, and $S(I_2/2)=\log2$. Therefore the mutual informations are $2\log2$ and $\log2$, respectively, as stated.
